article.title: Why More Features Can Make a Model Less Useful
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Adding features to a machine-learning model can improve predictive performance, but more is not always better. A feature has value only if it provides useful information at the time a decision must be made and can be maintained reliably in production. One major risk is leakage. A variable may contain information that becomes available only after the outcome or after the decision point. It can make offline accuracy look excellent while being unusable in a real campaign. Stability is another concern. A feature based on a temporary promotion, a changing system code, or a fragile external feed may work during training but shift sharply later. Even when predictive power remains, maintenance cost can rise. Every additional data source needs ownership, quality checks, refresh logic, access control, and failure handling. Complex features can also increase latency. A real-time decision system may not be able to wait for an expensive aggregation or remote lookup. Explainability matters in many business settings as well. A slightly more accurate model with hundreds of opaque or redundant variables may be harder to review, debug, and communicate than a simpler model with stable signals. Correlated features can spread importance across multiple variables and make explanations less intuitive. More features also create more opportunities for training-serving skew, where the data calculated during model development differs from the data available in production. Feature selection should therefore consider incremental predictive value alongside operational value. Teams can compare performance with and without a feature group, test stability across time, inspect missingness, and estimate computation and maintenance costs. They should verify that every feature has a clear timestamp and can be reproduced at scoring time. Regularization can control statistical complexity, but it does not solve data governance or leakage. The best production model is not necessarily the model with the highest offline metric. It is the model that provides enough predictive value while remaining timely, stable, understandable, and affordable to operate. Feature engineering should be treated as part of system design rather than a competition to create the largest possible input table. Analysts should state the population, observation window, assumptions, and decision point before interpreting the result. A useful review separates the observed pattern from the mechanism that may have produced it and from the action that should follow. This discipline makes the analysis easier to reproduce, challenge, and communicate to stakeholders.
